Triggers.value: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened

Maladaptive Strategies.value: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings
I try to push them out of my mind
keep mind occupied all the time

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me

vignette: As an urban planner in a busy city, Nguyen often found herself drawn to the serenity of nature reserves on her days off. But it was precisely these environments that now transported her back to the war-torn landscapes she had witnessed as a relief worker years ago. The sight of certain trees or rock formations triggered vivid memories of the makeshift camps and destroyed villages she had seen, sending her spiraling into a mix of emotions. When she came across old photos from that time on social media, it was like opening Pandora's box - she felt overwhelmed by flashbacks, where the past suddenly became indistinguishable from the present. When these episodes occurred, Nguyen tried to shake them off through physical activity or distraction. She had developed a habit of self-harm as a release mechanism for her emotions, often without realizing the severity of what she was doing in the heat of the moment. However, this coping strategy only led to more difficulties - when memories surfaced, they seemed even more real and intense than before. Moreover, every time Nguyen attempted to recount her experiences, she struggled to articulate them clearly; words failed her as if someone else had lived through those moments, not her. The feeling of being disconnected from her own memories was further exacerbated by the fear that these recollections could resurface at any moment. Her hypervigilance during sleep made restful nights a rarity - Nguyen needed to stay alert for potential threats in case another flashback struck. When she did drift off into sleep, nightmares often followed, leaving her jolted awake with an intense startle response to even the slightest movement nearby. It was as if her body had become programmed to react to perceived dangers around every corner. Nguyen's attempts at mental distraction only seemed to fuel this cycle of anxiety and memory disconnection. Her preoccupation with avoiding triggers inadvertently heightened their potency, making everyday situations like walking through a park or watching news coverage feel perilous. She also became intensely aware of any shouting nearby - it served as an alarm that her past experiences were about to encroach on the present once more. The irony was not lost on Nguyen; in trying to escape these memories and threats, she had inadvertently created a feedback loop where they only intensified over time. Lately, even the smallest triggers left her feeling like she was losing control - it was this spiraling sense of helplessness that finally pushed her to seek professional help. Though uncertain about what lay ahead in therapy, Nguyen knew one thing for sure: she needed to break free from these suffocating patterns and reconnect with her own story before they consumed her completely. Her partner had been increasingly worried about the toll all this was taking on their relationship and Nguyen's overall well-being - it was partly their concern that finally prompted Nguyen to take action. Now, as she stepped into therapy for the first time, the memories still lingered like an uninvited guest, refusing to be silenced or ignored. It remained to be seen whether the journey ahead would allow her to repossess these lost moments of her life and reintegrate them into a cohesive narrative - one that could finally grant her some measure of peace.
